title: String Pattern Matching

steps.title: Text and pattern
steps.content: String pattern matching asks whether a smaller pattern occurs in a larger text, and often where it occurs. A simple algorithm checks possible starting positions one by one.
steps.example: Pattern 'cat' occurs in text 'educate' at the substring 'cat'.

steps.title: Count a match
steps.prompt: Does the pattern 'aba' occur in the text 'ababa'?
steps.explanation: The substrings at indices 0–2 and 2–4 are both 'aba'.

steps.title: Understand the naive approach
steps.content: The naive search compares the pattern at each possible text position. If the text has length n and the pattern length m, worst-case time is O(nm).
steps.tip: Do not stop after the first mismatch if you still need to check later starting positions.

steps.title: Count candidate starts
steps.prompt: A text has length 8 and a pattern has length 3. How many possible starting positions can be checked?
steps.explanation: Valid starts are 0 through 8−3 = 5, giving 6 positions.

steps.title: Reuse previous comparisons
steps.content: Efficient algorithms such as Knuth–Morris–Pratt preprocess the pattern so that after a mismatch, they can skip comparisons already known to match. This improves worst-case search to O(n+m).
steps.example: KMP uses a prefix table to decide how far the pattern can shift without rechecking matched characters.

questions.prompt: What is the main goal of string pattern matching?
options: Find occurrences of a pattern in text
questions.explanation: Pattern matching searches for a smaller sequence inside a larger text.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time of naive matching for text length n and pattern length m?
questions.explanation: The naive algorithm may compare up to m characters at each of about n positions.

questions.prompt: How many possible start positions exist for n=10 and m=4?

questions.explanation: KMP builds a prefix/failure table from the pattern.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of KMP?
questions.explanation: KMP scans the text and pattern in linear time overall.

learning_objectives: Define pattern and text positions clearly.
Understand why repeated comparisons can be expensive.
Recognize prefix-based approaches such as KMP at a high level.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A match at one alignment means the whole text is searched.
common_misconceptions.correction: A matcher must test all candidate start positions or use a valid skip rule.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A mismatch always means move one character.
common_misconceptions.correction: Advanced matchers use prior matched information to skip safely.
KMP uses prefix/suffix structure, not hashing.

worked_examples.title: Naive match
trace: Align at index 0; compare a,b,a: match.
Continue at index 1; compare b against a: mismatch; index 2 matches.
worked_examples.explanation: Naive matching checks each possible alignment.

worked_examples.title: Count alignments
worked_examples.input: Text length n=8, pattern length m=3
trace: Possible starts range from 0 to n-m.
Each may compare up to m characters.
worked_examples.explanation: Repeated character comparisons can make naive matching quadratic.

worked_examples.title: KMP intuition
trace: Build longest proper prefix that is also suffix for each prefix.
On mismatch, reuse that prefix information.
Avoid rechecking text characters already known to match.
worked_examples.explanation: KMP uses prefix information to move the pattern without losing possible matches.

company_applications.practice: Trace alignments and explain prefix/suffix reuse.
State the naive complexity and edge cases.
Understand KMP preprocessing and linear-time guarantee.

srs_cards.question: What should you remember about String Pattern Matching?
srs_cards.answer: Define pattern and text positions clearly. Trace naive substring matching. Understand why repeated comparisons can be expensive. Recognize prefix-based approaches such as KMP at a high level.

srs_cards.question: What mistake should you avoid in String Pattern Matching?
srs_cards.answer: A matcher must test all candidate start positions or use a valid skip rule.
